description: How to make and weigh an argument: the kinds of inference, what makes one valid, how evidence and burden of proof work, the arts of rhetoric and debate, and the rules of thumb (razors) for choosing between explanations. The fallacies are in fallacies.json.

concepts.title: Argument
concepts.summary: Reasons offered in support of a conclusion. An argument isn't a quarrel: it's a claim, the grounds for it, and the step that connects them, laid out so someone else can check each piece.

concepts.title: Deduction
concepts.summary: Reasoning where the conclusion is forced by the premises: if they're true, it cannot be false. It gives certainty, but only about what was already contained in what you started with.

concepts.title: Induction
concepts.summary: Reasoning from cases to a general claim: the sun has risen every day, so it will rise tomorrow. It can never be certain, but it's how nearly all everyday and scientific knowledge is built.

concepts.title: Abduction
concepts.summary: Inference to the best explanation: the grass is wet, so probably it rained. It starts from a surprising observation and proposes what would make it unsurprising, which is how detectives and diagnosticians work.

concepts.title: Validity
concepts.summary: An argument is valid if its conclusion follows from its premises by form alone. Validity is about the structure, not the truth of the claims, so a valid argument can still have false premises.

concepts.title: Soundness
concepts.summary: A sound argument is valid and has true premises, so its conclusion is guaranteed to be true. Checking the form is only half the job; the other half is asking whether each premise is actually so.

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.summary: Whatever makes a claim more or less likely to be true. Good reasoning weighs evidence by how directly it bears on the claim, how reliable its source is, and how well the claim survives the alternatives.

concepts.title: Burden of Proof
concepts.summary: The duty to back up a claim falls on whoever makes it, not on whoever doubts it. Who carries the burden shapes a debate before a word of evidence is offered.

concepts.title: Steelmanning
concepts.summary: The opposite of a straw man: restate the other side's view in the strongest, most persuasive form before answering it. If you can't make their case well, you don't yet understand what you disagree with.

concepts.title: Principle of Charity
concepts.summary: Interpret what someone says in the most reasonable way available. It assumes they're probably rational and making sense, and it stops a disagreement from being won by misreading.

concepts.title: Fallacies
concepts.summary: Patterns of bad reasoning that look persuasive. Knowing their names doesn't win arguments, but it lets you notice, in your own thinking first, when a conclusion is being carried by something other than its reasons.

concepts.title: Rhetoric
concepts.summary: The art of persuading through speech and writing. It's neutral in itself: the same tools that dress up a weak case can clarify a strong one, and knowing them makes you harder to fool.

concepts.title: Ethos, Pathos, Logos
concepts.summary: Aristotle's three ways to persuade: by the speaker's credibility (ethos), by stirring feeling (pathos), and by the reasoning itself (logos). Most real persuasion mixes all three.

concepts.title: Socratic Method
concepts.summary: Teaching and testing ideas by asking questions rather than making statements. Each answer is probed until a hidden assumption or contradiction shows itself, which the person then discovers for themselves.

concepts.title: Dialectic
concepts.summary: Progress through the meeting of opposing views. A claim and its counterclaim are held against each other until something better, which keeps what was right in both, emerges.

concepts.title: Devil's Advocate
concepts.summary: Arguing against a position you may share, to test it. Done in good faith it exposes weak spots before someone else finds them; done carelessly it's just a way to avoid committing.

concepts.title: Debate
concepts.summary: A structured exchange of arguments on a proposition. Formal debate trains the skill of arguing either side well, and separates the strength of a case from the conviction of whoever presents it.

concepts.title: Occam's Razor
concepts.summary: Among explanations that fit the facts equally well, prefer the one with fewer assumptions. It's a guide to where to look first, not a proof that the simple answer is true.

concepts.title: Hanlon's Razor
concepts.summary: Never attribute to malice what is adequately explained by carelessness or ignorance. It's a check on the instinct to assume bad intent, and it usually improves both the conversation and the guess.

concepts.title: Sagan Standard
concepts.summary: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. The more a claim conflicts with everything else we have good reason to believe, the stronger the proof it needs before it should move us.

concepts.title: Hitchens's Razor
concepts.summary: What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence. It's a blunt way of saying that the burden of proof sits with the claimant, and that a bare assertion isn't an argument.

concepts.title: Syllogism
concepts.summary: The classic three-line deduction: all humans are mortal; Socrates is human; so Socrates is mortal. Two premises share a middle term, and the conclusion follows from how the categories nest.

concepts.title: Modus Ponens
concepts.summary: If P then Q; P; therefore Q. The most basic valid step in logic: affirm the condition, and you may affirm what follows from it.

concepts.title: Modus Tollens
concepts.summary: If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P. Deny the result and you must deny the condition. It is the logical form of a counterexample, and of most scientific refutation.
